summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: Berkshire Hathaway Energy is the largest privately held utility group in the corpus and the one that publishes its data-center book as a single contracted number — approximately 11,000 MW of data-center load 'in-service or in varying stages of construction' across its utilities, 91 percent of it with Aaa–Aa3 counterparties, against a 2025 data-center peak of just over 2,200 MW (about 8 percent of system peak) and a 4,500–5,700 MW peak projected for 2030 — while its lead AI-load utility, NV Energy, has become the corpus's clearest case of a franchise being asked for more than it has: about 22 GW of inquiries and about 6 GW of signed Rule 9 infrastructure agreements against a 2025 system peak of roughly 8,200 MW, answered on May 7, 2026 with a 2026 integrated resource plan (PUCN Docket 26-05007) that asks for 5,405 MW of battery storage and 4,370 MW of solar entirely through power purchase agreements, 1,223 MW of gas turbines at Fort Churchill, and a form Large Load Electric Service Agreement for any load of 25 MW or more — and, on July 24, a lawsuit to keep its largest prospective customer, Tract, in front of the commission rather than an arbitrator. The parent's rule is Abel's: serve the hyperscalers 'if there was no impact to the rates'. BACKGROUND. Des Moines, Iowa; wholly owned by Berkshire Hathaway Inc. since the 2024 buy-out of the Scott family's remaining stake, and an SEC registrant only because of its registered debt (one share of common stock outstanding, no dividend, no earnings call, no consensus). 2025: assets $148.3B, revenue $26.2B, earnings on common shares $4,066M ($4,054M adjusted), 38,800 MW of owned generation (49 percent non-carbon), 216,300 miles of electric and 49,900 miles of gas transmission and distribution, 9.4 million customers, 23,900 employees, $33.6B of 2026–2028 capital ($33.3B in the 10-K table). The operating companies: PacifiCorp (Rocky Mountain Power and Pacific Power; 2.1 million customers in six western states; selling its Washington service area to Portland General Electric for $1.9B), MidAmerican Energy (Iowa; 838,000 electric customers; industrial load 61 percent of retail sales), NV Energy (Nevada Power and Sierra Pacific Power; 1.5 million electric customers), BHE Pipeline Group (Northern Natural Gas, BHE GT&S, Kern River — about 15 percent of U.S. gas consumed), Northern Powergrid (UK), BHE Transmission (AltaLink; BHE U.S. Transmission) and BHE Renewables (5,488 MW). Credit: A3/A- at the parent; Nevada Power A2/A; MidAmerican Aa2/A; PacifiCorp A3/BBB+ after $2.85B of accrued wildfire losses. Collection gap: brkenergy.com's HTML pages are blocked to automated readers and SEC hosts refused the sandbox, so BHE's own FY2025 10-K and Q1/Q2 2026 10-Qs were not read — the 10-K's 'contracted load' wording, its capex table and BHE-basis quarterly segment earnings are taken from Berkshire's 10-Qs, the 2026 investor presentation and Industrial Info; nvenergy.com renders no server-side content, so the LLESA's commercial percentages (minimum demand, minimum energy, the customer-specific generation charge) are the customers' reserved Exhibit G items and were not read; PacifiCorp's Utah large-load contract counterparty and docket, the Fort Churchill turbine OEM, the Sierra Solar battery supplier and Fleet's engine supplier were not found; executive photographs and most bios were not retrievable.
ecosystemRole: We assess Berkshire Hathaway Energy as the corpus's PPA-side utility buyer: NV Energy's 2026 plan puts every one of its 5,405 MW of new batteries and 4,370 MW of solar under power purchase agreements with developers (23 PPAs, counterparties confidential), so the storage sellers in this file reach NV Energy through the developers who won its 2024 all-source RFP (198 bids, 21,019 MW, 12,634 MW of it storage) and the named 2024 IRP counterparties — Arevia's Libra (700 MW / 2,800 MWh), NextEra's Dry Lake East, 174 Power Global's Boulder Solar III — not through a utility purchase order; the exceptions are the utility-owned Reid Gardner (220 MW / 440 MWh, Energy Vault EPC, BYD cells) and Sierra Solar (400 MW / 1,600 MWh, supplier undisclosed, 2026) batteries and PacifiCorp's IRP proxies of 4,154 MW of four-hour lithium and 523 MW of 100-hour iron-air by 2045. Basis: the 2026 IRP application (Docket 26-05007), the NV Energy IRP fact sheet ('more than 5,400 MW of battery storage through power purchase agreements'), the investor presentation's $0.2B of storage capex inside $33.6B, and the 2025 IRP Update. For the gas vendors the doors are the 1,223 MW of Fort Churchill aeroderivative and frame turbines (2030–2032), NV Energy's 400 MW Valmy peakers under evaluation (2028), MidAmerican's 520 MW two-turbine peaker (siting certificate November 2025; 'about 700 MW' in the Corporate Overview) and PacifiCorp's 1,370 MW of combined-cycle and 853 MW of frame-turbine proxies — none with an OEM named. For the developers and hyperscalers in the corpus BHE is Amazon's, Google's, Vantage's and Tract's Nevada utility (five LLESA dockets, 26-05026 through 26-05030), Amazon's Oregon adversary at the OPUC, Microsoft's, Google's and Meta's Iowa utility under ten-year load commitment agreements, and — through Tract — the first utility in this file to sue a data-center developer over who decides how the grid gets built.

productsAndServices.name: NV Energy regulated service and the large-load framework — Rule 9 agreements, the form LLESA (Docket 26-05007) and the Clean Transition Tariff
productsAndServices.description: Nevada Power Company (southern Nevada, 1.1 million electric customers, 2025 peak 6,168 MW, 5,391 MW owned) and Sierra Pacific Power Company (northern Nevada, 0.4 million electric and 0.2 million gas customers, 2025 peak 2,073 MW, 1,617 MW owned) are vertically integrated, PUCN-regulated utilities outside any RTO capacity market (WEIM participants; PacifiCorp's EDAM membership from May 2026 is the group's first day-ahead market). 2025 retail sales were 32,913 GWh plus 5,790 GWh of distribution-only service to Nevada's 704B exit customers. Data-center peak demand was about 400 MW in 2025; the 2026 IRP forecasts 3,600 MW of peak data-center load by 2030 (contracted fully-bundled and distribution-only customers plus about 14 percent of study-phase requests), about 22,000 MW of interest inquiries and about 6 GW of signed Rule 9 agreements — the existing mechanism, under which a large customer advances the cost of its distribution and transmission infrastructure and commits to minimum usage, but which 'does not address generation'. The 2026 IRP (application dated May 6, docketed May 7, 2026; statutory decision deadline December 2, 2026) therefore files a form Large Load Electric Service Agreement for 'new and existing accelerated large customer loads of 25 MW or greater' (Wells direct, Q23): a Maximum Demand and ramp schedule, minimum billing for demand and energy, a customer-specific generation charge recovered before any plant enters rate base, a termination payment (mitigated if a commensurate customer assumes the load) and ESA Customer Security under objective credit standards; NV Energy asked for the form to be deemed approved by September 18, 2026 on the energy-supply-plan timeline. Five customers filed eight LLESAs totalling more than 3.3 GW by 2032 — Amazon Data Services at Sparks (26-05026), Fleet Data Centers / Tract's PR RNO and SV RNO at McCarran (26-05027; 25 years post-COD, minimum bill 90 percent of contracted per New Project Media), Vantage Data Centers NV11 (26-05028), Novva Las Vegas / Proton NLV (26-05029; 300-month term, ramp up to 48 months) and VIP Landco / Prologis (26-05030) — each reserving the minimum-demand and minimum-energy percentages, the generation charge, the rates, the termination payment and the security calculation for PUCN determination (Exhibit G). The Clean Transition Tariff (Docket 24-05023, filed June 7, 2024 with Google's Sierra Pacific agreement, approved March 2025) lets an eligible customer buy bundled service from a named new clean resource at a customer-specific charge — Google's is Fervo's 115 MW Corsac Station 2 (January 2030); a second CTT deal with Ormat and an Amazon geothermal agreement (May 2026) followed. Governor Lombardo's Executive Order 2026-005 (September 17, 2026) directs the PUCN to 'determine instrument and terms ensuring data centers bear full service costs with no burden on other ratepayers' and to set load-reduction requirements for grid emergencies.

productsAndServices.name: NV Energy 2026 IRP supply plan — 5,405 MW of battery PPAs, 4,370 MW of solar, 1,223 MW of Fort Churchill gas and the $4.2B Greenlink lines
productsAndServices.description: The 2027–2046 Triennial IRP and 2027–2029 Energy Supply Plan (Docket 26-05007) asks the PUCN to approve 23 power purchase agreements adding about 4,550 MW of renewables (4,370 MW of paired solar and 180 MW of geothermal) and 5,405 MW of battery output capacity — 'new paired and standalone BESS PPA projects by 2031' — plus 1,223 MW of NV Energy-owned gas at Fort Churchill (Additions 1 and 2, 401 MW of aeroderivative turbines each, June 2030 and June 2031; Addition 3, 421 MW of frame turbines, June 2032), $13.0M of early-development funding for a 2034 combustion turbine, 171 MW of demand-side management, and a third amendment to the Libra PPA adding 200 MW of storage in contract years 21–25. Project names in the technical appendices include Amargosa Energy Center Phases 1 and 2, Castor Storage, Commerce Station Energy Storage, Coyote Energy 1, Dry Lake East Energy Storage II, Fish Springs Ranch Energy Storage, Hot Pot Energy Center and Winston Solar; counterparties are confidential. The plan rests on the 2024 all-source RFP (198 bids, 73 unique projects, 21,019 MW including 12,634 MW of storage; a 15-project, 8,000 MW-plus shortlist for 2027–2030) and a load forecast 47 percent higher in annual GWh than the 2024 IRP's over twenty years; the January 2026 stakeholder briefing said 'total new thermal may exceed 3 GW in next decade' with the earliest new turbine in 2029–2030, and the IRP warns that RPS compliance 'will be challenging for several years due to load growth' (2025 renewables 47.5 percent against a 34 percent standard). Already approved from the 2024 IRP and its amendments: Sierra Solar, 400 MW of solar and a 400 MW / 1,600 MWh four-hour battery, utility-owned (Sierra Pacific 90 percent, Nevada Power 10 percent; storage 2026, solar 2027; about $1.5B); Libra Solar and Storage (Arevia Power, 700 MW + 700 MW / 2,800 MWh, 25 years, $34.97/MWh and $13,350/MW-month, December 2027); Dry Lake East (NextEra Energy Resources, 200 + 200 MW / 800 MWh, December 2026); Boulder Solar III (174 Power Global, 128 + 128 MW, June 2027); the Dodge Flat 150 MW four-hour battery addition (20-year PPA signed September 27, 2025; July 2027); the North Valmy coal-to-gas conversion (522 MW total, 261 MW NV Energy share; coal ended at end-2025) and 400 MW of Valmy peaking generation 'under evaluation' for May 2028 (about $573M approved December 20, 2024, Docket 24-05041). Greenlink Nevada — Greenlink West (350 miles of 525 kV, 725 MW of import capacity, Fort Churchill to Northwest in 2027 and to Harry Allen in 2028) and Greenlink North (235 miles, 800 MW, 2028) with two 345 kV common ties — carries a combined expected cost of $4.2B, of which 50 percent of the West line's costs to date entered rates in the September 2025 order; NV Energy's capital plan is $3.0B in 2026, $2.8B in 2027 and $1.9B in 2028.

productsAndServices.name: PacifiCorp (Rocky Mountain Power and Pacific Power) — large-load rules in Utah, Oregon and Wyoming, the 2025 IRP Update and the Washington sale
productsAndServices.description: PacifiCorp serves 2.1 million retail electric customers across 141,500 square miles in Utah, Wyoming, Idaho (Rocky Mountain Power) and Oregon, Washington and California (Pacific Power), with 11,873 MW of owned generation, 17,500 miles of transmission and 5,200 employees; retail sales were 59,212 GWh in 2025 (+1.3 percent) and are forecast +2.2 percent in 2026 and +2.0 percent in 2027 'primarily due to increased data center growth'. Its large-load position is a set of state rules rather than one tariff: Utah's 2025 SB 132 (loads of 100 MW or more within five years; a 90-day utility evaluation; three service pathways including closed private generation) 'requires large load customers to fully support marginal costs while enabling faster regulatory reviews', and PacifiCorp filed its first contract under it — 'hundreds of MWs', 'nearly $1 billion in estimated net benefits', approval anticipated April 2026, counterparty and docket not found; Oregon's 2025 HB 3546 (the POWER Act) requires new data centers over 20 MW to fully support all costs, and PacifiCorp has proposed Schedule 401 as a large-energy-use-facility class (ADV 1790 / UE 463) after UE 433 added two charges for very large customers — but 'negotiations on additional sites have stalled', and Amazon Web Services filed an OPUC complaint in November 2025 alleging PacifiCorp failed its service obligation, which the company disputes ('six to eight months' absent settlement); Wyoming and Utah tariffs added charges for unused demand. The book: Oregon 'over 7,000 MWs of data center load' pursued with 784 MW under contract; Utah and Wyoming 'approximately 2,000 MWs of additional opportunities' by 2030; the 2025 IRP Update's Table 6.1 shows 839 MW (east) and 592 MW (west) of large load energized at end-2025 and 839 / 1,054 MW contracted at maximum ramp. The 2025 IRP Update (March 31, 2026) added 'substantial new gas resources' — 1,370 MW of proxy combined-cycle and 853 MW of proxy frame turbines by 2045 — with 4,154 MW of four-hour lithium and 523 MW of 100-hour iron-air storage, 3,705 MW of wind, 2,477 MW of utility solar and TerraPower's Kemmerer Unit 1 (Natrium, 345 MWe boostable to 500 MWe, end-2031), and dropped new wind and solar after 2027 'largely driven by the July 4, 2025 repeal of major portions of the IRA'. On February 17, 2026 PacifiCorp agreed to sell its Washington service area — the 477 MW Chehalis gas plant, 234 MW Marengo and 94 MW Goodnoe Hills wind, and distribution serving about 140,000 customers around Yakima and Walla Walla — to Portland General Electric (51 percent) and Manulife Infrastructure Fund III for a $1.9B base price, closing 'first half of 2027' after WUTC, OPUC and FERC approval; it also signed term sheets to sell 8,904 Oregon customers to three cooperatives and will sell-leaseback the Boardman-to-Hemingway line to a BHE affiliate (about $1.1B, November 2027). Wildfire is the constraint on all of it: $2.85B of probable losses accrued through June 30, 2026 ($2.3B paid), the James class verdict reversed and remanded April 8, 2026, the Oregon Supreme Court's argument on November 3, 2026, a $575M federal settlement, a $2.55B letter-of-credit facility, S&P at BBB+ and a March 2026 CreditWatch for junk.

productsAndServices.name: MidAmerican Energy (Iowa) — the load commitment agreement, 800 MW of solar, a 520–700 MW peaker and the hyperscaler campuses
productsAndServices.description: MidAmerican serves 838,000 electric and 811,000 gas customers in Iowa, Illinois, South Dakota and Nebraska from 12,243 MW of net owned capacity (8,231 MW non-carbon; 45 percent below the U.S. average rate at 7.83 cents/kWh) inside MISO. It is the group's data-center utility of record: 2025 retail sales rose 9.6 percent (industrial +12–13 percent) 'primarily due to continued load growth from data centers', industrial load is 61 percent of retail GWh, data centers were about 8 percent of Iowa peak load at the May 2026 annual meeting with 'visibility to grow that by 50% or more over the next five years', and the 2026–2027 forecast (+5.2 and +3.4 percent) 'includes only signed contracts with large-load customers that fund all incremental transmission and substation investments'. Its instrument is the Load Commitment Agreement — 'binding load ramp schedules and a minimum monthly charge over 10 years, regardless of actual usage', with exit penalties, and customer funding of every incremental substation and transmission line; no IUC large-load tariff docket exists (EEI's Iowa entries are Alliant's). Named campuses are third-party: Microsoft in West Des Moines ('Project Alluvion', about 200 MW), Google at Council Bluffs ($5.5B) and, from August 3, 2026, an agreement to explore a 900-acre Salix site, Meta at Altoona, Apple at Waukee. Supply: the Solar Reliability Project, up to 800 MW at six Iowa sites under advance ratemaking approved September 2025 (ROE 9.95 percent; 2026–2028); a two-turbine gas peaker with an IUC siting certificate (November 2025) of 520 MW — the Corporate Overview calls the Adair County plant 'approximately 700 megawatts' for 2028–2029 and a third-party report 518 MW at Orient, so three figures are on the record; Wind PRIME (603 MW total by 2027) and $1.5B of repowering expected to keep 100 percent of production tax credits for ten years; MISO Tranche 1 projects of $1.6B (2028–2034). 2026–2028 capex is $8.9B — new generation $4.6B including $1.1B of turbines and $1.9B of renewables. Iowa's profit cap is 10.3 percent with 90 percent of excess returned; MidAmerican filed a natural gas rate case (about 5 percent) on July 7, 2026.

productsAndServices.description: BHE Renewables owns or is building 5,488 MW across 26 facilities in 11 states — 13 wind farms (2,545 MW), 1,690 MW of solar (Solar Star, Topaz, Agua Caliente), four gas plants (898 MW), CalEnergy's 345 MW of Imperial Valley geothermal and 10 MW of hydro — plus the Occidental direct-lithium-extraction demonstration plant (complete mid-2026; commercial decision by year-end). The December 2025 Grande Prairie blade failure idled 141 of 200 turbines there and 31 of 36 at Marshall until March 2026; Rio Bravo (238 MW of wind) was bought in March 2025. BHE Renewables earned $585M in 2025 and carries $1.0B of the 2026–2028 plan.

strategyRead: (High confidence) We assess that NV Energy has moved the equipment decision for its entire storage build to developers, and that a storage seller reaches it only through the 2024 RFP shortlist and the 2026 IRP's confidential PPA counterparties. Basis: the 2026 IRP application (5,405 MW of BESS output, 'new paired and standalone BESS PPA projects by 2031', 23 PPAs), the fact sheet's 'through power purchase agreements', the $0.2B storage line in BHE's $33.6B plan (down from $907M in the prior plan per Industrial Info), and the two owned exceptions (Reid Gardner, Sierra Solar) already contracted. We expect the PUCN's December 2, 2026 order to approve the PPAs largely as filed, because the plan's open-capacity target (≤500 MW short by 2031) leaves no slack to reject them.

(High confidence) We assess that the LLESA framework, not the IRP's resource list, is the document that decides how much of the 22 GW of Nevada inquiries becomes load — and that its commercial terms will be set by the PUCN under a governor's order rather than negotiated. Basis: the form LLESA's reserved provisions (minimum demand and energy percentages, generation charge, termination payment, security) left blank by all four filing customers; the September 18 deemed-approval request; EO 2026-005's instruction to the PUCN to ensure 'no burden on other ratepayers'; and NV Energy's own statement that timing, upfront investment and customer-protection measures 'may cause some customers to seek options outside of NV Energy's service territory'. The Tract temporary gas plants (362 MW approved September 17) are the first evidence of that exit already happening.

(High confidence) We assess that the NV Energy–Tract litigation is a jurisdictional contest, not a commercial one, and that the utility will win the forum question: the suit asks a court to keep supply adequacy, cost allocation and resource-plan treatment in front of the PUCN instead of a private arbitrator, and the PUCN itself approved Tract's bridging plants a week before the executive order gave it the mandate the suit presupposes. Basis: the July 24, 2026 complaint (Washoe County CV26-02142), Tract's June 2026 arbitration demand under the 2024 Reno Power agreements, the 26-05027 LLESA docket, and the September 17 conditional approval of 26-04026/27. The corpus's Tract dossier carries the developer's side; the Nevada Independent's account is used here for the utility's.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that PacifiCorp's data-center book will grow in Utah and Wyoming and stall in Oregon through 2027, and that the Washington sale, the co-op sales and the B2H sale-leaseback are wildfire-liquidity transactions first. Basis: the presentation's 'negotiations on additional sites have stalled' under Oregon's HB 3546 against a first Utah SB 132 contract with 'nearly $1 billion' of net benefits and about 2,000 MW of Utah/Wyoming opportunity; AWS's OPUC complaint; the liquidity plan's modeling of $1.9B (April 2027) and about $1.1B (B2H) of proceeds against 'CMO No. 11 @ 50%' damages; and S&P's March 2026 CreditWatch. The 2025 IRP Update's gas proxies (2,223 MW) and 4,677 MW of storage proxies are a decade-long book with no procurement door open in 2026.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that MidAmerican's ten-year Load Commitment Agreement is the most durable large-load instrument in the group because it is a contract rather than a tariff or a form, and that Iowa will see the next named hyperscaler expansion (Google Salix) before Nevada sees its next LLESA approved. Basis: 'includes only signed contracts', the 10-year minimum monthly charge regardless of usage, the +65 percent capex plan concentrated on 800 MW of solar and a 520–700 MW peaker with pre-approved returns, and no tariff docket or litigation in the record. The three peaker figures (520 MW siting certificate; 'approximately 700 megawatts'; 518 MW Orient) are recorded as a conflict, not resolved.

(Low confidence) We assess that BHE Renewables will announce a behind-the-meter data-center generation project of 1 GW or more before the end of 2027, and that it would buy gas turbines rather than batteries for it. Basis: the presentation's 'site diligence and preliminary development activities are ongoing at several prospective sites, which may be capable of serving projected demands scaling to 1 GW or more', the Pipeline Group's 'behind the meter' framing, the Alberta and Montana customer discussions, and the parent's rule that hyperscaler service must have 'no impact to the rates' — which a nonregulated affiliate satisfies by construction. No site, customer, technology or filing has been found.

policyExposure.regime: Wildfire liability — PacifiCorp (Oregon James class action; state statutes)
policyExposure.exposure: PacifiCorp has accrued $2.85B of probable wildfire losses through June 30, 2026 ($2.3B paid; $719M of bonds posted), with 'reasonably possible' material additional losses; cumulative James verdicts of about $1.23–1.25B for roughly 200 plaintiffs were reversed and remanded by the Oregon Court of Appeals on April 8, 2026, the circuit court stayed the remaining damages trials, and the Oregon Supreme Court hears argument on November 3, 2026. S&P placed PacifiCorp on CreditWatch for junk in March 2026 after $305M and $34M verdicts; Moody's cut it to Baa2 unsecured in July 2025. State responses: Utah SB 224 (2024) noneconomic caps and a wildfire fund; Wyoming HB 192 (zero noneconomic liability); Idaho SB 1183; Oregon's punitive bills SB 926 and SB 1553 defeated; Washington's HB 2275 fund failed in 2026; California's SB 254 fund does not include PacifiCorp.
policyExposure.mitigation: $575M federal settlement (February 2026); $150M Warren Allen settlement; a $2.55B letter-of-credit and matching surety facility; the Washington sale ($1.9B), Oregon co-op sales and B2H sale-leaseback (~$1.1B) in the liquidity plan; $3.4B of wildfire prevention since 2019 plus $2.8B through 2028; Abel: 'PacifiCorp is not an insurer of last resort'.

policyExposure.regime: Nevada large-load framework — form LLESA (Docket 26-05007), Rule 9, EO 2026-005 and the RPS
policyExposure.exposure: Nevada has no large-load statute (the 2025 session passed AB452 on fuel-cost sharing and SB442 on disconnection data, nothing on data centers); the LLESA is a PUCN contract framework filed with the 2026 IRP, its commercial percentages reserved for the commission, with a deemed-approval request for September 18 and a statutory IRP deadline of December 2, 2026. Governor Lombardo's EO 2026-005 (September 17, 2026) directs the PUCN to ensure data centers 'bear full service costs with no burden on other ratepayers', to set grid-emergency load-reduction requirements and to consider an investigatory docket; GOED abatement conditions and a 'Responsible Speed to Power Plan' (December 31, 2026) follow. The IRP itself warns that RPS compliance (34 percent in 2025 against 47.5 percent delivered) 'will be challenging for several years due to load growth', and the PUCN denied a public session on the IRP in August 2026 over advocates' objections.
policyExposure.mitigation: Advances under Rule 9 for distribution and transmission; the customer-specific generation charge ahead of rate base; termination payments and security in the LLESA; the Clean Transition Tariff for customers buying new clean resources; the utility's suit to keep Tract's cost allocation before the commission.

policyExposure.regime: Utah SB 132 (2025) and Oregon HB 3546 (POWER Act, 2025) — PacifiCorp large-load statutes
policyExposure.exposure: Utah's SB 132 applies to loads of 100 MW or more within five years, gives the utility 90 days to evaluate whether it can serve without significant investment, and allows contracts with large-scale generation providers over utility transmission or closed private generation systems — PacifiCorp calls it enabling 'faster regulatory reviews and isolation of costs and benefits while allowing limited direct access'. Oregon's HB 3546 (Chapter 323, effective on passage, sunset January 2, 2035) requires the OPUC to create a 'large energy use facilities' class, allocate costs to it and require contracts; PacifiCorp says negotiations 'have stalled over disputes on the implementation' and faces AWS's service-obligation complaint. Schedule 401 (ADV 1790 / UE 463) is proposed; UE 433 added two charges for very large customers.
policyExposure.mitigation: The first Utah SB 132 contract ('hundreds of MWs', ~$1B net benefits); unused-demand charges in Oregon, Utah and Wyoming; reduced line-extension credits, accelerated customer funding, enhanced security and tax gross-ups.

policyExposure.exposure: Berkshire's 10-K: the OBBBA 'accelerates the phase-out of clean electricity production and investment tax credits and establishes new sourcing requirements applicable to facilities commencing construction after December 31, 2025'; BHE 'currently does not believe these items will significantly impact its business in the near term', but PacifiCorp's 2025 IRP Update dropped new wind and solar after 2027 'largely driven by the July 4, 2025 repeal of major portions of the IRA', NV Energy's 2024 RFP shortlist prioritized 'viability of project securing tax credits' and projects 'with no federal nexus', and MidAmerican expects repowered wind to keep '100% of production tax credits for 10 years' based on current law. BHE's effective tax rate was −76.2 percent in 2025 on wind PTCs, with $1.4B of cash tax benefits from the parent; Reid Gardner received about $100M of IRA credits including an energy-community adder. No FEOC statement was found; Reid Gardner's cells are BYD's, and NV Energy's 5,405 MW of new storage sits with PPA developers.
policyExposure.mitigation: Berkshire's consolidated tax appetite; PPA structures that leave sourcing and credit-qualification risk with developers; safe-harbor positioning in the RFP selection criteria.

policyExposure.regime: Western markets — no capacity market; CAISO EDAM (PacifiCorp from May 1, 2026), WEIM (NV Energy), MISO (MidAmerican)
policyExposure.exposure: BHE's western utilities face no capacity auction; resource adequacy is an IRP obligation (NV Energy's open-capacity goal ≤500 MW short by 2031; the Western Resource Adequacy Program referenced in PacifiCorp's IRP Update). PacifiCorp launched CAISO's Extended Day-Ahead Market on May 1, 2026 (FERC tariff approval August 29, 2025; $5.42M of gross benefits by July 30; PGE joins October 2026) and has drawn more than $1.2B from the Western EIM since 2014. MidAmerican sits in MISO, where the Tranche 2.1 award to the BHE/AEP venture and $1.6B of Tranche 1 Iowa projects drive transmission capex; no BHE commentary on MISO's 2026/27 auction price was found. FERC's June 18, 2026 large-load show-cause orders name the RTOs, not BHE's western utilities.
policyExposure.mitigation: EDAM and WEIM dispatch savings; MISO capacity accreditation for the 800 MW solar and 520 MW peaker; interruptible large-load contracts historically at PacifiCorp.
